Five Ways This Curriculum Prepared You for What's Coming

Gartner says 33% of enterprise software will include agentic AI by 2028. If you've been paying attention, you're already ahead.

By Chris O'Hara · 8 min read

A stat landed last week that should make every product marketer sit up. Gartner predicts that 33% of enterprise software will include agentic AI by 2028—up from less than 1% in 2024. And here's the kicker: 15% of day-to-day work decisions will be made autonomously.

Not "AI-assisted." Not "AI-recommended." Autonomously.

33%
of enterprise software will include agentic AI by 2028
— Gartner, August 2026

Let that sink in. The CRM you use every day? It's getting an agent. The marketing automation platform? Agent. The ERP system your finance team guards like a dragon hoards gold? Agent. These won't be chatbots you summon when you need help. They'll be colleagues that act—analyzing data, making recommendations, executing tasks—while you sleep.

For product marketers, this isn't a distant future. It's Tuesday.

The question is whether you're ready. And if you've been working through this curriculum, you are—even if you didn't realize that's what we were building toward.

The Shift Nobody Talks About

Here's what most "AI for marketers" training gets wrong: they teach you to use AI tools. Prompt engineering. ChatGPT tricks. How to make Claude write your emails faster.

That's table stakes. That's learning to drive a car in 1995.

The real shift isn't AI as a tool you use—it's AI as a layer that permeates everything. It lives inside the software you already run. It makes decisions on your behalf. It talks to other agents. Your job isn't to operate the AI; it's to architect the system in which AI operates.

That's what we've been training you for. Not the prompt. The architecture.

Five Ways You're Already Ahead

1. You Know How to Build for Two Audiences

Unit 2 didn't just teach you about GEO—Generative Engine Optimization. It fundamentally reframed who your content is for. Human buyers, yes. But also the AI systems that increasingly mediate what those humans see.

When 72% of holiday shoppers are now consulting ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini for product recommendations—a stat from this week's Optimove report—the game has changed. Your positioning, your messaging, your competitive differentiation: all of it needs to be legible to machines, not just humans.

You've been practicing this. Most PMMs haven't even heard of it yet.

2. You've Built Personas That Agents Can Actually Use

Unit 10 pushed hard on a simple premise: most B2B personas are fiction. Workshop artifacts. PDF files that live in SharePoint and die in obscurity.

The personas you learned to build are different. They're grounded in behavioral signals—what buyers actually do, not what they claim in interviews. They're structured in ways that AI systems can operationalize. When an agentic CRM needs to decide how to prioritize an account or what message to send, it needs something more than "CFO Carol values ROI."

The behavioral persona frameworks from Unit 10? That's what agents need. You're already building them.

3. You Understand Competitive Intelligence at Machine Speed

Competitive intelligence used to be a quarterly exercise. Pull the Gartner MQ. Update the battlecard. Brief the sales team.

That cadence is dead. Unit 3 introduced you to real-time competitive monitoring—AI agents that track pricing changes, sentiment shifts, hiring patterns, and product launches continuously. You saw BattleCoach in action at last week's Office Hours: a tool that generates battle briefs on demand, handles live objections, and simulates competitive scenarios.

The future of competitive intelligence isn't a document. It's a conversation with an agent. You've already had that conversation.

4. You Can Enable Sales When Everyone Has AI

Here's a problem nobody's solved yet: what happens to sales enablement when every company's reps have AI assistants?

If everyone can generate a pitch deck in seconds, the deck stops being the differentiator. If everyone has an AI that summarizes call notes and suggests next steps, execution speed becomes table stakes. The competitive moat moves upstream—to the quality of your positioning, the specificity of your use cases, the depth of your competitive insight.

Unit 5 walked you through this. Your sales enablement strategy isn't about making content faster. It's about making the inputs to AI systems better than your competitors' inputs. Your battlecards, your personas, your messaging frameworks—they become the training data for your company's AI-powered selling motion.

You get that now. Most enablement teams are still counting asset downloads.

5. You've Practiced Working With AI, Not Just Using It

Every lab in this curriculum forced you to work alongside AI tools. The Competitive Analyzer. The Persona Builder. The PMM Assistant. These weren't tutorials—they were simulations of how your job will actually work when every enterprise tool has an agent embedded.

The meta-skill isn't prompt engineering. It's workflow architecture. How do you structure a process so that AI handles the repeatable parts while you focus on judgment and strategy? How do you review AI outputs without becoming a bottleneck? How do you maintain quality when the machine is doing 80% of the work?

These are the questions that will define the next two years. You've been practicing answers.

What Comes Next

The Gartner stat—33% by 2028—sounds like a prediction. But predictions are just permission structures. They give executives cover to invest, vendors cover to build, and practitioners cover to experiment.

The real timeline is faster. Salesforce has Agentforce. HubSpot launched Agent Hub. ServiceNow, Microsoft, SAP—everyone's shipping agentic capabilities now, not in two years.

The PMMs who thrive in this environment won't be the ones who "learned AI." They'll be the ones who learned to work in systems where AI is ambient—present in every tool, every workflow, every decision.

You've been doing that for months now. Units 11 and 12 will take you further. But the foundation is set.

When your colleagues are scrambling to figure out what "agentic" even means, you'll already be building.
